title: What India’s Protests Reveal About the Future of Liberalism
gist: In a Foreign Affairs interview Pratap Bhanu Mehta argues India's youth protests over exam leaks and voter-roll revision are the most consequential challenge to Modi since 2014, tests of independent institutions, and part of a broader global crisis of liberalism and shared prosperity.

insights.claim: Indian youth protests that began in July over an exam leak have linked exam leaks, the Election Commission's special intensive revision of electoral rolls, and a broader critique of authoritarianism into one package that attacks the foundations of the regime rather than single policies.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: The protests are a structural legitimacy challenge to Modi, raising Indian political-risk uncertainty.
insights.locator: The other thing that I think has been surprising

insights.claim: Student leaders have been detained repeatedly and nearly 40,000 police and paramilitary were deployed in Delhi, 245 trains into Delhi canceled and 47 metro stations shut on protest day, which Mehta reads as the government acknowledging the movement's power regardless of its size.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: The scale of the state response signals government fear and a coercion-heavy playbook.
insights.locator: just to give a little anecdote, 245 trains into Delhi were canceled

insights.claim: Mehta expects the government to double down on authoritarianism, using repeated arrests, extended custody and claims of foreign funding, while hoping the electoral-roll controversy fades as more voters are included.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Expect more repression and a managed-narrative approach before the Uttar Pradesh election.
insights.locator: On the stick side, frankly

insights.claim: The next big test of the government's legitimacy is the Uttar Pradesh election early next year; the government hopes a win will restore legitimacy and let people forget the protests as they did the farmers' protest.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: The Uttar Pradesh result is the key near-term political catalyst for India.
insights.locator: The next big test of the government's legitimacy

insights.claim: Elections and exams are the two institutions through which the Indian state signals fairness and equality, and exams are the only ticket to social mobility for most lower-middle-class and poor students.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Perceived corruption of these institutions provokes disproportionate unrest.
insights.locator: For elections, the case is straightforward

insights.claim: The Election Commission's special intensive revision flagged about 130 million names for possible removal, and Mehta lists changes versus 2002: more identity requirements, loss of the presumption of prior inclusion, central software that could send notices overriding local verification, and in West Bengal about 2.7 million voters placed on a disputed list days before the election.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: The scale of potential disenfranchisement is the core driver of the protest movement.
insights.locator: And in this process, 130 million names

insights.claim: The Supreme Court allowed the West Bengal election to proceed with disputed voters barred from voting, saying they could vote in the next election if eligible, which Mehta calls astonishing and which contributed to suspicion of incompetence or manipulation.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Judicial deference weakens institutional checks, a governance risk for India.
insights.locator: In this case, what was astonishing

insights.claim: The protests are among the first recent revolts attributable directly to the failure of independent institutions, and the central demand is the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an audit or cancellation of the SIR.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Institutional credibility is the axis of the contest.
insights.locator: Look, first of all, these protests are a result

insights.claim: The 'Cockroach Janta Party' name came from an offhand remark by the Chief Justice of India about unemployed lawyers, and its social media handle gained 22 million followers within a week.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast social-media mobilization can scale in India.
insights.locator: the Cockroach Janta Party

insights.claim: Repeated exam-paper leaks, and the centralization of exams in a national testing agency, made the central government directly responsible and forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: The movement has already won a cabinet-level resignation, a first for the Modi government according to Mehta.
insights.locator: So the answer is very simple

insights.claim: India's headline growth is about seven percent but benefits the top ten percent while the state funds welfare for the bottom 25 to 30 percent, leaving a large middle failing to move into high-productivity, high-wage jobs; graduate unemployment is roughly 23 to 25 percent.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: K-shaped growth and a jobs gap underlie political instability despite strong GDP.
insights.locator: But the growth has a particular character

insights.claim: Many protesters are middle-class children of the greatest beneficiaries of liberalization, anxious about downward mobility, which is rare in Indian protest movements.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Middle-class downward-mobility anxiety broadens the political base of discontent.
insights.locator: But the remarkable thing about this movement

insights.claim: The protests have already forced the Election Commission to modify its revision procedures, simplify them and reach out to excluded voters; forcing the chief election commissioner's resignation would be hard because it would implicitly call the election process's legitimacy into question and could embolden the opposition and invite defections within government.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Modi's control depends on officials answering only to the government; institutional accountability would weaken that.
insights.locator: So there's one big success the protest already has

insights.claim: The protests handed the opposition a tangible issue, as every opposition party now doubts the SIR, and Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi have joined street politics, though the opposition still must prove it can act as a cohesive coalition capable of governing.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Opposition revival potential depends on tactics and coalition-building, not rallies.
insights.locator: It's definitely an opportunity

insights.claim: Liberal crisis in both India and the U.S. shares three features: a failure of shared prosperity despite strong headline growth (about 2.5 percent in the U.S., seven percent in India), populist leaders arguing that liberal checks and balances block the people's will, and legitimacy claimed through nationalism.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Populist executive-power politics rest on inequality and oligarchy resentment, a common macro-political driver.
insights.locator: Actually, I think there are striking parallels

insights.claim: The challenge of shared prosperity also afflicts authoritarian systems: China's labor share of the prosperity generated over 20 to 30 years does not look spectacularly better than that of the United States.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Social-contract dissatisfaction is global, not specific to liberal democracies.
insights.locator: So there is something about the social contract

insights.claim: Globalization was not a cosmopolitan alternative to liberal nationalism but a means of realizing it, and a zero-sum competition for primacy between China and the U.S. is unlikely to sustain liberal values or global public goods.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: A zero-sum world order undermines global public goods and cooperation, raising fragmentation risk.
insights.locator: Globalization was not a kind of cosmopolitan alternative

insights.claim: The U.S. and China, the only two countries controlling most advanced technologies particularly AI, are seen by the rest of the world as having gone rogue by weaponizing sanctions and export controls, so other countries sign trade deals with each other and seek supply chain resilience.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Middle powers hedging against both superpowers supports intra-middle-power trade and supply-chain diversification.
insights.locator: The United States certainly is engaged in reckless wars

insights.claim: Ten years ago Asian discussion was which power to hedge against, China or the United States; now the discussion is hedging against both.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Strategic hedging against both great powers is now mainstream among middle powers.
insights.quote: Now, the discussion is we need to hedge against both.
insights.locator: I mean, 10 years ago, the discussion in Asia

insights.claim: Mehta contends the rest of the world lacks the power to check and balance the two superpowers, but wants to build institutional architecture as inoculation against both.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Middle-power coalition building is aspirational and limited in power terms.
insights.locator: Now, the brute fact of the matter

insights.claim: Modernity's persistent tension between freedom and self-determination on one hand and bureaucracy, capitalism and the nation-state on the other (Weber's iron cage) is a universal condition that nobody has come to terms with.
insights.speaker: Pratap Bhanu Mehta
insights.so_what: Explains recurrent backlash against institutions across political systems.
